stemBlocks.value: A double bar chart shows library visits by students in Grades 7 to 11 over two terms. Term 1: 40, 50, 45, 60, 70. Term 2: 60, 60, 55, 75, 80. (a) How many Grade 9 visits were recorded in Term 2? (b) Calculate the total number of visits recorded in Term 2. (c) Which grade showed the greatest increase from Term 1 to Term 2? (d) Calculate the percentage increase in visits by Grade 10 students. (e) Describe ONE trend shown by the chart and give ONE possible inference.
Think first: Read both bars for each grade before answering anything — every part compares the pair.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p085-q13 from workbook page 85.

solutionSteps.instruction: Read both bars for every grade.
Subtract Term 1 from Term 2 for each grade.

contentBlocks.value: Result: Grade 7 shows the greatest increase

solutionSteps.instruction: Find the percentage increase for Grade 10.

strategyBlocks.value: Tabulate the two terms grade by grade, add the Term 2 column, subtract to find each grade's increase, and use increase ÷ Term 1 × 100 for the percentage.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (a) 55 visits  (b) 330 visits  (c) Grade 7, with an increase of 20 visits  (d) 25%  (e) Trend: every grade made more visits in Term 2 than in Term 1, and the number of visits generally rises with grade level. Inference: library use grew across the school in Term 2, possibly because of examination preparation, which would also explain why the higher grades visit most.

whyThisWorks.value: A double bar chart places two related frequencies side by side, so a difference can be read directly as the gap between neighbouring bars. Turning those differences into percentages of the original value makes changes comparable between grades: a rise of 15 means far more for a grade starting at 40 than for one starting at 70.

commonErrors.misconception: Adding both terms when only the Term 2 total is wanted.
